specStatements.text: (HT only) Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength.
(HT only) Some effects, for example refraction, are due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances.
Students should be able to construct ray diagrams to illustrate the refraction of a wave at the boundary between two different media.
(HT only) Students should be able to use wave front diagrams to explain refraction in terms of the change of speed that happens when a wave travels from one medium to a different medium.
Required practical activity 10: investigate how the amount of infrared radiation absorbed or radiated by a surface depends on the nature of that surface.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 4.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

concepts.definition: When a wave meets a substance and its energy is transferred into that substance rather than continuing through it. The wave does not emerge on the far side, and the internal energy of the substance rises.
When a wave passes through a substance and continues on the other side of it. A substance that transmits a wave allows it through with little of its energy being absorbed.
When a wave meets a boundary and is sent back into the substance it came from, instead of passing into the second substance.

The change in direction of a wave as it crosses the boundary between two different substances at an angle to the normal. A ray diagram shows it as the incident ray and the refracted ray making different angles with the normal.

concepts.term: Variation of these effects with wavelength
concepts.definition: How a substance behaves towards electromagnetic waves is not a single fixed property of that substance. The same substance may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves of different wavelengths in different ways: glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet reaching it, and brick transmits radio waves but not visible light.

concepts.term: Difference in velocity as the cause of refraction
concepts.definition: Electromagnetic waves travel at different velocities in different substances. Some effects, refraction among them, are due to that difference in velocity: if the velocity of the wave is the same in both substances, no refraction occurs at the boundary between them.

A construction line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the point where the ray meets it, shown as a dashed line in a ray diagram. Every angle in a ray diagram is measured between a ray and the normal, never between a ray and the boundary.

concepts.term: Angle of incidence and angle of refraction
concepts.definition: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of refraction is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal on the far side of the boundary.

A straight line with an arrow on it showing the direction in which the wave is travelling. A ray diagram of refraction shows the incident ray up to the boundary, the normal at that point, and the refracted ray continuing into the second medium.

Draw the boundary, then the normal as a dashed line where the incident ray meets it. A ray passing from air into glass or water bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence. A ray passing from glass or water into air bends away from the normal. A ray that travels along the normal is not bent and carries straight on.

A line joining points on a wave that are all at the same point in their cycle, for example a line along a crest. Wave fronts are drawn at right angles to the direction in which the wave is travelling, and the distance between one wave front and the next is one wavelength.

When a wave front reaches the boundary at an angle, the end that crosses first changes speed first while the rest of the front is still travelling at the original speed. The front is therefore turned, and the direction of travel of the wave changes. In the medium in which the wave travels more slowly the wave fronts are drawn closer together, because the wave moves a shorter distance in each cycle; the frequency of the wave is unchanged.

concepts.term: Dependence of infrared absorption and emission on the surface
concepts.definition: Every surface both absorbs and emits infrared radiation, but the amount depends on the nature of the surface. Matt, dark surfaces are the best absorbers and the best emitters of infrared radiation. Shiny, light-coloured surfaces are the poorest absorbers and the poorest emitters, and the best reflectors.

A sealed metal cube whose vertical faces carry different surfaces, typically matt black, matt white, shiny black and shiny silver. It is filled with hot water so that all four faces are at the same temperature, and an infrared detector held the same distance from each face in turn compares the radiation each surface emits.

concepts.term: Control variables in required practical activity 10
concepts.definition: Only the nature of the surface may be changed. The distance between the surface and the detector or heater, the time for which readings are taken, the starting temperature, and the position and height of the detector must all be kept the same, or a difference in the readings cannot be attributed to the surface.

AT 1 covers the use of appropriate apparatus to make and record a range of measurements accurately. In this activity that means measuring distance with a ruler, time with a stopwatch, and temperature with a thermometer or infrared detector, and recording those readings to the resolution the instrument allows.

AT 4 covers making observations of the effects of the interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter. In this activity that means observing how infrared radiation interacts with surfaces of different nature — how much each surface absorbs when it faces a radiant heater, and how much each emits when it is hot.

concepts.term: WS and MS opportunities in this practical
concepts.definition: The activity also gives opportunities to develop working scientifically skills, such as identifying control variables, judging the resolution and repeatability of measurements and evaluating the method, and mathematical skills, such as tabulating readings, calculating means and plotting temperature against time. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

misconceptions.question: Why does a wave change direction when it crosses a boundary at an angle?
misconceptions.correct: Because the wave travels at a different velocity in the second substance; refraction is due to that difference in velocity.
misconceptions.misconception: The wave bounces off the edge of the new material, or the new material pushes the wave sideways — its speed does not come into it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Refraction is taught as a bending of light long before the wave picture is available, so students remember the shape of the diagram and invent a mechanical cause for it. Nothing in the ray diagram itself shows a change of speed.
misconceptions.correction: Refraction happens because the velocity of the wave differs in the two substances. If a wave travelled at the same velocity in both, it would cross the boundary without changing direction, however steeply it met the boundary.

misconceptions.question: Which way does a ray bend when it crosses a boundary between two media?
misconceptions.correct: It bends towards the normal going from air into glass or water, and away from the normal going from glass or water into air.
misconceptions.misconception: Light always bends towards the normal whenever it goes into a different material.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every worked example met first is air into glass, so students learn one arrow direction and treat it as the rule for all boundaries rather than as one case of it.
misconceptions.correction: The direction of bending depends on which way the wave crosses the boundary. Entering glass or water from air it bends towards the normal; leaving glass or water into air it bends away from the normal.

misconceptions.question: What happens to a ray that meets the boundary along the normal?
misconceptions.correct: It carries straight on into the second medium without any change of direction.
misconceptions.misconception: Any ray that goes into a new material must bend, so a ray along the normal bends a little too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn 'refraction happens at a boundary' as an unconditional rule and apply it to the one case where the geometry gives no change of direction.
misconceptions.correction: At an angle of incidence of zero there is no change of direction, so the ray is drawn as a straight line through the boundary. On the Higher tier, note that the wave still changes speed — it simply has no sideways effect to produce.

misconceptions.question: Where is the angle of refraction measured from?
misconceptions.correct: From the normal — the dashed line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the point the ray meets it.
misconceptions.misconception: The angle is measured between the ray and the surface of the block, because that is the line you can actually see.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The boundary is a real drawn line and the normal is only a construction line, so the eye is drawn to the boundary. Both angles then come out as the complement of the correct value.
misconceptions.correction: All angles in a ray diagram are measured between a ray and the normal. A diagram must show the normal as a dashed line at 90° to the boundary, with the angles marked from it.

misconceptions.question: What changes when a wave front diagram shows a wave entering a slower medium?
misconceptions.correct: The speed falls and the wave fronts are drawn closer together, so the wavelength is smaller; the frequency is unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: The wave fronts get closer together because the frequency of the wave has dropped in the new medium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Closer fronts look like a more rapid wave, and students link spacing to frequency rather than to wavelength. The source, not the medium, is what fixes the frequency.
misconceptions.correction: The frequency is set by the source and does not change at the boundary. The speed changes, so from v = fλ the wavelength changes with it, and that is what the changed spacing of the wave fronts shows.

misconceptions.question: If a substance transmits one electromagnetic wave, does it transmit them all?
misconceptions.correct: No. The same substance may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength.
misconceptions.misconception: Glass is transparent, so all electromagnetic waves pass through it; a material is either see-through or it is not.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday judgements about materials are made with the eye, which senses only one narrow band of wavelengths, so 'transparent' feels like a whole-material property.
misconceptions.correction: Transparency belongs to a material and a wavelength together. Glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet reaching it, while a brick wall stops visible light but transmits radio waves.

misconceptions.question: Which surface emits the most infrared radiation at a given temperature?
misconceptions.correct: The matt black surface. Good absorbers of infrared radiation are also good emitters of it.
misconceptions.misconception: Matt black surfaces soak up radiation and hold onto it, so it is the shiny silver surface that gives out the most.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Absorbing and emitting sound like opposites, so students expect a surface that is good at one to be poor at the other, and 'black absorbs everything' is learned first.
misconceptions.correction: The same property of the surface governs both. A matt black surface is the best absorber and the best emitter; a shiny silver surface is the poorest absorber and the poorest emitter.

misconceptions.question: Does the colour and finish of a surface matter for infrared radiation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. How much infrared a surface absorbs, emits or reflects depends on the nature of that surface.
misconceptions.misconception: Black and silver only look different to our eyes, so surface colour can only affect visible light, not infrared.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour is defined for students by vision, and infrared is invisible, so the two seem to belong to separate worlds.
misconceptions.correction: Infrared is absorbed, emitted and reflected at a surface just as light is, and the readings in this practical show matt dark surfaces and shiny light surfaces behaving quite differently.

misconceptions.question: What must be kept the same when comparing the faces of a Leslie cube?
misconceptions.correct: The distance from the detector, the position and height of the detector, the timing, and the temperature of the water.
misconceptions.misconception: As long as each face is tested with the same detector, the readings can be compared however the detector is placed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat 'same equipment' as the whole of a fair test and overlook that the intensity of the radiation received falls off sharply with distance from the surface.
misconceptions.correction: Only the nature of the surface may change. Move the detector nearer to one face and its reading rises whatever that face is like, so the comparison no longer tests the surface at all.

misconceptions.question: How are wave fronts drawn in relation to the direction of travel?
misconceptions.correct: At right angles to the direction of travel, one wavelength apart, each front joining points at the same point in their cycle.
misconceptions.misconception: Wave fronts are just rays under another name, so they are drawn along the direction the wave is going.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are lines on a wave diagram and both are introduced as ways of representing the same wave, so the perpendicular relationship between them is easily lost.
misconceptions.correction: A ray points along the direction of travel; a wave front lies across it, at 90° to it. That is why turning the fronts at a boundary turns the direction of travel.

misconceptions.question: Does absorption of an electromagnetic wave depend on the wave alone?
misconceptions.correct: No. It depends on the substance as well as on the wavelength: different substances treat the same wavelength differently.
misconceptions.misconception: Whether a wave is absorbed is fixed by the type of wave, so a wave that is absorbed by one material is absorbed by every material.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Waves are learned as a list of named types with fixed properties and uses, which invites students to attach behaviour to the wave and forget the material it meets.
misconceptions.correction: It takes both. The specification states that different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength — the substance and the wavelength together decide what happens.

misconceptions.question: Does the wavelength of a wave change when it enters a different medium?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The speed changes and the frequency does not, so the wavelength changes with the speed and the wave fronts are drawn at a new spacing.
misconceptions.misconception: Wavelength belongs to the wave itself, so it stays the same whatever medium the wave is in; only the speed can change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Waves are first met as a fixed shape with a labelled wavelength, so wavelength feels like an identity tag for the wave rather than a quantity tied to the speed in the medium.
misconceptions.correction: Only the frequency is fixed by the source. With v = fλ, a change of speed at the boundary forces a change of wavelength, which is exactly what the changed spacing of the wave fronts shows.

misconceptions.question: A student moves the detector nearer for one face of a Leslie cube. What is wrong with the results?
misconceptions.correct: A control variable has changed, so the difference in the readings cannot be attributed to the nature of the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: The results are spoilt because the water in the cube cooled down while the readings were being taken.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students memorise a stock list of criticisms for practical work and offer one of them instead of checking which variable was actually allowed to change.
misconceptions.correction: Cooling is a genuine limitation, and is why the faces should be tested quickly, but here the specific fault is that distance changed alongside the surface, so two variables changed at once.

mcqs.stem: A sheet of glass transmits almost all of the visible light that reaches it, but absorbs much of the ultraviolet. What does this show?

options.text: A material that looks clear must transmit every electromagnetic wave that reaches it.
options.rationale: A student who treats transparency as a whole-material property reads 'glass is see-through' as a claim about all wavelengths.

options.text: Whether a substance absorbs or transmits a wave can depend on the wavelength of that wave.
options.rationale: Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength, and glass acting differently on two wavelengths is exactly that.

options.text: Ultraviolet is absorbed by every substance it meets, whatever that substance is.
options.rationale: This attaches the behaviour to the wave alone and ignores the substance, which is the error the statement is written against.

options.text: Glass reflects the ultraviolet at its surface, so none of it enters the glass at all.
options.rationale: Reflection is a different effect from absorption; the question says the ultraviolet is absorbed, which means its energy is transferred into the glass.

mcqs.stem: A mobile phone signal (radio waves) passes through the brick wall of a house, but visible light from outside does not. Which statement explains this best?

options.text: Brick reflects radio waves back outside, and the phone detects those reflected waves.
options.rationale: Reflected waves would be sent back outside the wall, so they could not reach a phone inside the house.

options.text: Radio waves are absorbed by every material, so brick makes no difference to them.
options.rationale: Fixing the behaviour to the wave alone; it also contradicts the signal arriving indoors at all.

options.text: One substance can transmit one wavelength while absorbing or reflecting another.
options.rationale: The behaviour of brick towards electromagnetic waves varies with wavelength: it transmits the long-wavelength radio waves and stops visible light.

options.text: A material that stops light must stop all electromagnetic waves reaching it.
options.rationale: The student judges the wall by eye and generalises 'not see-through' to the whole spectrum.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about substances and electromagnetic waves matches the specification?

options.text: A given substance treats all wavelengths of electromagnetic wave in the same way.
options.rationale: The direct opposite of the statement, and it matches the everyday feeling that a material is either see-through or not.

options.text: Absorption is decided by the wave alone, so the substance it meets is irrelevant.
options.rationale: Students who learn the spectrum as a list of waves with fixed properties attach the behaviour to the wave.

options.text: Substances may absorb or reflect electromagnetic waves, but they can never refract them.
options.rationale: Refraction is one of the four behaviours named, and it is the one this section goes on to treat in detail.

options.text: Substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves in ways varying with wavelength.
options.rationale: This is what the specification states: all four behaviours are possible, and how a substance behaves varies with the wavelength of the wave.

mcqs.stem: Refraction of an electromagnetic wave at a boundary between two substances is due to which of the following?

options.text: The wave bouncing off the boundary between the two substances at an angle.
options.rationale: A mechanical cause invented to fit the bent-arrow shape of the ray diagram; it also describes reflection, not refraction.

options.text: The difference in the velocity of the wave in the two substances either side of it.
options.rationale: The specification gives refraction as an example of an effect due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances.

options.text: The difference in the frequency of the wave in the two substances either side of it.
options.rationale: Students who think the medium changes the frequency reach for frequency wherever a change at a boundary is being explained.

options.text: The second substance absorbing some of the energy carried by the incoming wave.
options.rationale: Absorption reduces the energy transmitted; it does not by itself change the direction in which a wave travels.

mcqs.stem: A wave crosses at an angle into a second substance in which it travels at exactly the same velocity as in the first. What happens at the boundary?

options.text: It bends towards the normal, because a ray entering any new substance bends that way.
options.rationale: The air-to-glass case is learned as a universal rule, so the student answers before checking what the velocities are doing.

options.text: It carries on in the same direction, as there is no difference in velocity to refract it.
options.rationale: Refraction is due to the difference in velocity of the wave in the two substances. With equal velocities that cause is absent, so the direction is unchanged.

options.text: It bends away from the normal, because the second substance is a different material.
options.rationale: Being a different material is not the cause; without a difference in velocity there is no reason for the direction to change either way.

options.text: It is reflected at the boundary, since the wave cannot pass into a new material.
options.rationale: The bouncing picture of what happens at a boundary, applied here to block the wave from entering at all.

mcqs.stem: A ray of light travels through air and meets a glass block at an angle of incidence of 40°. In a correct ray diagram, the refracted ray inside the glass is drawn:

options.text: bent away from the normal, at an angle of refraction larger than 40° from the normal.
options.rationale: The direction of bending is reversed: this is what happens when a ray leaves glass and enters air.

options.text: bent towards the normal, at an angle of refraction measured as 40° from the boundary.
options.rationale: The bending is right but the angle is read from the boundary rather than the normal, giving the complement of the true value.

options.text: straight on through the block, since the ray meets a flat boundary between two media.
options.rationale: A ray only carries straight on when it meets the boundary along the normal; at 40° incidence it must change direction.

options.text: bent towards the normal, at an angle of refraction smaller than 40° from the normal.
options.rationale: A ray passing from air into glass bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is less than the angle of incidence.

mcqs.stem: A ray of light inside a glass block reaches the far surface at an angle of incidence of 25° and passes out into the air. In the ray diagram the emerging ray is:

options.text: bent away from the normal, so the angle from the normal is greater than 25°.
options.rationale: A ray passing from glass into air bends away from the normal, so the angle of refraction exceeds the angle of incidence.

options.text: bent towards the normal, because refraction always turns a ray towards the normal.
options.rationale: The one-rule-fits-all error: the air-to-glass direction of bending is applied to a glass-to-air boundary.

options.text: bent away from the boundary, so the angle from the boundary is greater than 25°.
options.rationale: The angle is taken from the glass surface rather than from the normal, which is the line all angles must be measured from.

options.text: unchanged in direction, because the ray is leaving the block rather than entering it.
options.rationale: Refraction occurs at any boundary crossed at an angle to the normal, whichever way the wave is going.

mcqs.stem: A ray of light travelling through air meets the flat surface of a water tank along the normal. How should the ray diagram be drawn?

options.text: The ray is drawn bending slightly towards the normal as it enters the water.
options.rationale: 'Refraction happens at every boundary' is applied without checking the geometry of this particular case.

options.text: The ray is drawn bending away from the normal as it enters the water.
options.rationale: Same error as bending towards the normal, with the bend guessed the other way; both assume a bend must occur.

options.text: The ray is drawn continuing straight on into the water without changing direction.
options.rationale: At an angle of incidence of zero there is no change of direction, so the ray is drawn as a straight line through the boundary.

options.text: The ray is drawn reflected back along its own path into the air.
options.rationale: Light striking a water surface along the normal is transmitted into the water; it is not sent back along its path.

mcqs.stem: Which line must be added to a refraction ray diagram before the angles of incidence and refraction can be marked on it?

options.text: A dashed line at right angles to the boundary where the incident ray meets it.
options.rationale: This is the normal, and both the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction are measured from it.

options.text: A dashed line along the boundary itself, from which both angles are measured.
options.rationale: The visible boundary is used as the reference line instead of the normal, so both angles come out as complements.

options.text: A dashed line at right angles to the incident ray at the point it meets the boundary.
options.rationale: This is a wave front rather than a normal; the two perpendicular construction lines are readily confused.

options.text: A dashed line continuing the incident ray onwards into the second medium.
options.rationale: That line is only useful for showing how far the ray has been turned; the angles themselves are measured from the normal.

mcqs.stem: A wave front diagram shows water waves crossing at an angle into a region where they travel more slowly. Why does the direction of travel change?

options.text: The frequency of the wave falls in the new region, which turns each wave front round.
options.rationale: The frequency is set by the source and is unchanged; students blame frequency for anything altering at a boundary.

options.text: The end of each wave front that crosses first slows first, so the front is turned round.
options.rationale: One end of the front changes speed while the other is still travelling faster, which swings the front and so turns the direction of travel.

options.text: The wave fronts point along the direction of travel and are dragged round by the boundary.
options.rationale: Wave fronts are confused with rays; they lie across the direction of travel, not along it.

options.text: The wave fronts are reflected at the boundary and then re-enter the slower region.
options.rationale: Reflected fronts would travel back into the first region; they cannot account for the wave continuing onwards in a new direction.

mcqs.stem: In a wave front diagram, a wave passes from a medium where it travels quickly into one where it travels slowly. The wave fronts in the slower medium are drawn:

options.text: closer together than before, because the wave travels less far in each cycle.
options.rationale: The frequency is unchanged and the speed is lower, so each cycle covers a shorter distance: the wavelength, which is the spacing of the fronts, is smaller.

options.text: further apart than before, because the wave takes longer to complete each cycle.
options.rationale: The time for a cycle is fixed by the frequency and does not change; a slower wave covers less distance per cycle, not more.

options.text: closer together than before, because the frequency of the wave has been reduced.
options.rationale: The spacing is right but the reason is wrong — the frequency is unchanged, and it is the wavelength that has fallen.

options.text: at the same spacing as before, because the wavelength cannot change at a boundary.
options.rationale: Students who treat wavelength as a fixed label for the wave keep the spacing unchanged even though the speed has altered.

mcqs.stem: A Leslie cube is filled with hot water and an infrared detector is held the same distance from each face in turn. Which face gives the highest reading?

options.text: The matt black face, because good absorbers of infrared are also good emitters.
options.rationale: The nature of the surface governs both absorption and emission, and a matt black surface is the best at each.

options.text: The shiny silver face, because it releases the radiation instead of holding onto it.
options.rationale: Absorbing and emitting are treated as opposites, so the best absorber is expected to be the worst emitter.

options.text: Every face reads the same, because the colour of a surface only affects visible light.
options.rationale: Infrared is invisible, so students assume that how a surface looks cannot matter to it.

options.text: The matt white face, because pale surfaces give out the most heat when they are hot.
options.rationale: Matt white emits less than matt black; the pale colour makes it a poorer emitter, not a better one.

mcqs.stem: Two identical metal plates, one matt black and one shiny silver, are placed the same distance from a radiant heater for ten minutes. What is found?

options.text: The shiny silver plate rises to the higher temperature, as it holds in more infrared.
options.rationale: Confuses being a poor emitter with gaining energy; the silver plate also absorbs poorly, so it warms up least.

options.text: Both plates rise to the same temperature, as the surface finish affects only light.
options.rationale: Colour and finish are assumed to be visual properties with no bearing on invisible radiation.

options.text: Both plates rise to the same temperature, as they are made of the same metal.
options.rationale: The metal fixes how energy spreads within the plate, but it is the surface that decides how much infrared is absorbed.

options.text: The matt black plate rises to the higher temperature, as it absorbs more infrared.
options.rationale: A matt dark surface is the best absorber of infrared radiation, so it gains energy fastest and reaches the higher temperature.

mcqs.stem: A student compares the faces of a Leslie cube but holds the detector 5 cm from one face and 15 cm from the next. Why are the results not valid?

options.text: The detector gives readings in the wrong units when it is moved between the faces.
options.rationale: The units of a detector do not depend on where it is placed; the fault lies in the variable that has been allowed to change.

options.text: The water cools during the experiment, which is the only variable that has changed.
options.rationale: A stock criticism of the method is offered in place of naming the variable that was allowed to change.

options.text: Distance has changed as well as the surface, so the difference cannot be attributed to the surface.
options.rationale: The reading falls as the detector is moved away, so with two variables changing at once the effect of the surface cannot be isolated.

options.text: Distance from the face makes no difference to the reading, so the test proves nothing.
options.rationale: The student who thinks placement is unimportant concludes the readings are still comparable and looks elsewhere for a fault.
